chunks: "Inductance is the property of a conductor that makes it oppose changes in the current through it.
When current flows, it creates a magnetic field, and that field links back through the circuit.
Inductance is how much magnetic flux linkage you get per amp: L equals N over I , measured in henries. The important part is what happens when the current changes.
A changing current means a changing flux, and Faraday's law says a changing flux induces a voltage. Lenz's law says that voltage pushes back against the change.
So you get v equals L di over dt : the faster you try to change the current, the bigger the voltage the inductor develops to fight it. I think of it as inertia for current.
A capacitor resists changes in voltage; an inductor resists changes in current.
And it stores energy in its magnetic field, 1 over 2 LI squared , which is exactly what buck and boost converters exploit.
Physically it depends on geometry and material: more turns, bigger loop area, and a high-permeability core all increase it, roughly L equals micro N squared A over .
And it's not just in coils. Every wire and PCB trace forms a loop with its return path, so everything has some parasitic inductance.
That's why fast edges cause ground bounce and ringing."
